thread.title: Apple's Tim Cook Wants to Focus on 'the Most Important Things'

title: Apple's Tim Cook Wants to Focus on 'the Most Important Things'
text:
Apple’s Tim Cook Wants to Focus on ‘the Most Important Things’ By Jan. 9, 2019 1:56 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Emmanuel Dunand/AFP/Getty Images Text size
Shares of Apple (AAPL) are still below the levels from which they fell after the company’s market-shaking announcement of disappointing iPhone sales in China to start the year. They have also shown signs of life more recently, rising this week.
Apple’s shares, recently up about 2% to near $154—though still down in 2019—have gained as the company has sought to demonstrate that it has charted a path toward growth by focusing on selling more services and worrying less about iPhone sales.
Earlier this week, at the Consumer Electronics Show, Apple’s software was a key component of product announcements made by other manufacturers , illustrating the company’s willingness to open its garden walls to make its services more widely available. It followed its downbeat guidance with an upbeat press release about services sales.
Perched on an Apple store bench just feet away from CNBC’s Jim Cramer, CEO Tim Cook sat Tuesday for a lengthy interview in which he insisted he wasn’t there to sell the stock. (“I try to sell a product,” Cook said. A transcript of the interview is on CNBC’s site.) Newsletter Sign-up
Cook, who said some of the company’s recent troubles in China were temporary, said a trade deal with Beijing was very possible, expressing optimism that a deal “will be good, not only for us, frankly, but I think more about the world in general.”
Major U.S. indexes were up recently as a round of U.S.-China trade negotiations closed. “The world needs a strong U.S. and China economy for the world economy to be strong,” Cook said.
But he was careful not to make any detailed statements that might be read as financial projections. He seemed determined to remind investors that the company can be both a hotbed of innovation and an investor-friendly enterprise that’s mindful of shareholder returns.
“Those are the most important things for us: innovation, customer satisfaction, and the overall size and loyalty of our customers,” Cook said.
He did say Apple would announce new services this year, adding that they would be “material over time.” Later, he characterized the company’s health-care efforts as poised to be “Apple’s most important contribution to mankind.”
Building the services profile through revamped or new offerings —or even acquisitions —is what many analysts consider a priority for Apple in 2019 and beyond.
“We continue to believe the services business, poised to exceed $50 billion in fiscal 2020, will be the ultimate driver for the next phase of the Apple growth story,” Wedbush analyst Daniel Ives wrote Wednesday. ”Better execution, a more innovative product strategy, larger M&A around content/more services, and losing pricing hubris will need to take place in Cupertino, with Cook’s chess moves over the coming months laying the groundwork to help get Apple out of its darkest chapter in the modern iPhone era.”
